question: A boy is found to have a right undescended testis at his six-week check. The testis is palpable at the superficial inguinal ring. At what age should orchidopexy ideally be performed, and why?

answers.text: At birth, because every month of delay causes irreversible damage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Surgery at birth is not recommended — testicular descent can still occur spontaneously up to six months of age, and the vas and vessels are extremely delicate in the neonatal period.

answers.text: Between 6 and 18 months, to protect spermatogenic potential and facilitate cancer surveillance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Current guidelines recommend orchidopexy between 6 and 18 months. Placing the testis in the scrotum early preserves germ-cell development and permits lifelong self-examination for the increased risk of testicular malignancy.

answers.text: At puberty, when the testis is larger and easier to mobilise

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting until puberty is too late — spermatogenic damage begins in the second year of life, and delaying repair substantially reduces fertility outcomes.

answers.text: Only if spontaneous descent has not occurred by age five

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Age five is too late; spontaneous descent beyond six months is uncommon, and surgery deferred past 18 months risks irreversible histological changes in the germinal epithelium.

overallFeedback.feedback: Orchidopexy should be performed between 6 and 18 months — after the window for spontaneous descent but before spermatogenic damage becomes irreversible. Puberty is far too late.
Correct. Orchidopexy at 6–18 months: maximises spermatogenic preservation and enables surveillance for the life-long elevated malignancy risk.
